chapters.title: Chapter 5: Recent Shocks and the Investor's Playbook

lessons.title: The Crisis Playbook: Warning Signs Every Indian Investor Should Track

body.text: You cannot predict the date of the next crisis. But almost every crisis in this course was preceded by the same small set of warning lights, and every one of them can be tracked with free, public Indian data.

children.text: This course has run from New York in 1929 to Zurich in 2023. The playbook is still being used. In early 2026, conflict in West Asia pushed energy prices up and put pressure on the rupee. India's forex reserves, which had touched a record $728.49 billion in late February, fell to $682.3 billion by 29 May as the RBI sold dollars to steady the currency. On 8 June 2026, the RBI opened a special swap window for FCNR(B) deposits from non-resident Indians. By 31 August, those deposits had brought in about $127 billion, and in the week of 4 September, reserves hit a new record of $785.71 billion.

That was the same diaspora playbook India used in 1998 and 2013, now at a far larger scale. This final lesson turns everything you have learnt into a practical dashboard: six warning lights, where to find the data, and how to read it.
Every Crisis in This Course, and Its Main Warning Light

body.caption: The main warning light behind each crisis

Mortgage securities funded with overnight repo that vanished
Rapid corporate lending, then evergreening, then gross NPAs peaking at 11.2%
Greece's misreported deficit and bonds priced almost like Germany's
A record current account deficit funded by portfolio money
China stock bust and yuan shock, 2015
A stock boom built on record margin lending, followed by capital flight
Long-term loans funded with short-term commercial paper
Off-budget LGFV borrowing repaid from land sales that later collapsed
About 73% of advances to a single borrower group

body.title: How often each warning light was the main cause across the 16 crises in this course

body.text: For India, the pattern has shifted. The crises of 1991 and 2013 were external: not enough dollars. The crises of the 2010s and 2018 were domestic: bad loans, fragile funding and concentration inside India's own financial system. A good dashboard watches both.

body.caption: The Indian investor's crisis dashboard
headers: Rule of thumb from this course

cells: Current account deficit as % of GDP; import cover; short-term external debt compared with reserves
RBI balance of payments releases and weekly statistical supplement; RBI Database on Indian Economy
The RBI has described a deficit of about 2.5% of GDP as sustainable; import cover under 3 months is a danger sign; reserves should at least cover short-term external debt
Foreign portfolio flows into Indian debt; NBFC reliance on commercial paper; debt fund holdings
NSDL FPI Monitor; company annual reports; AMC monthly portfolio disclosures
Money that can leave within a year should not be funding assets that take many years to pay back
Bank credit growing much faster than the economy; the RBI's review of the countercyclical capital buffer
RBI data on bank credit; RBI announcements on the countercyclical capital buffer
Basel guidance suggests building buffers once credit-to-GDP runs 2 percentage points above its long-run trend
Debt to equity of companies you own; margin and leveraged trading; bank and NBFC capital ratios
screener.in and annual reports; RBI Financial Stability Report
Wipeout point = capital ÷ assets. The thinner the cushion, the smaller the shock needed
Rating outlooks and rationales; restated accounts; auditor concerns; unrealised bond losses
Rating agency releases; stock exchange filings on NSE and BSE; bank annual reports
A AAA rating or a smooth track record is a starting point for questions, not a guarantee
Lending to one sector or borrower group; your own exposure to one bank, company or product
Bank annual report disclosures; your own portfolio statements
No single borrower, bank or product should be able to sink you, as HDIL sank PMC

children.text: Here is what some of the external warning lights showed recently. Numbers change every week or quarter, so treat these as an example of how to read the dashboard, and look up the latest figures before drawing any conclusion.

stats.label: Import cover, late May 2026
stats.context: Per the RBI Governor, on reserves of $682.3 billion

columns.label: India, mid-1991
points: Two to three weeks of import cover
Current account deficit of 3.1% of GDP in 1990-91
Government-set exchange rate and no current account convertibility

columns.label: India, 2026
points: Forex reserves of $785.71 billion in the week of 4 September
About 11 months of import cover in late May
Current account deficit of 0.6% of GDP in 2025-26
Market-determined rupee with RBI intervention, convertible on the current account since 1994

body.text: Strong external readings do not mean no risk. The 2018 NBFC crisis and the 2019 PMC Bank collapse both happened while India's reserves were comfortable. External strength protects against a 1991-style crisis. It does nothing to stop a lender with bad loans or a fragile funding model from failing.

body.title: Calculate Import Cover
body.prompt: A country has forex reserves of $700 billion and imports $840 billion of goods and services a year. Assuming imports run evenly through the year, how many months of imports can its reserves cover?
body.explanation: Monthly imports = $840 billion ÷ 12 = $70 billion. Import cover = $700 billion ÷ $70 billion = 10 months. Compare that with India in June 1991, when reserves covered just two to three weeks of imports. Economists generally treat about 3 months as the bare minimum.

body.title: Name the Rule
body.textWithBlank: The Guidotti-Greenspan rule says a country's forex reserves should at least cover its short-___ external debt, meaning debt due within one year.
body.explanation: Short-term external debt. The idea, proposed in 1999 after the Asian crisis, is that a country should be able to survive a full year without new foreign lending. India at end-March 1991 had short-term debt of 382.1% of its forex assets, nearly four times the rule's limit.

body.title: Which Light Is Flashing Brightest?
body.question: An emerging economy reports these readings. Which one most closely matches the warning sign that preceded India's 1991 crisis and the Asian crisis of 1997?
options: Inflation of 5%, slightly above the central bank's target
Short-term external debt equal to 180% of forex reserves
Bank credit growing in line with the economy
A stock market that fell 8% last quarter
body.explanation: Short-term external debt of 180% of reserves breaks the Guidotti-Greenspan rule badly: if foreign lenders stopped rolling over for a year, reserves could cover barely half of what is due. That was the core weakness in India in 1991 and in Thailand, Indonesia and Korea in 1997. Mildly high inflation and a market correction are worth watching, but they are not crisis signals on their own.

body.title: Read a Hypothetical Dashboard
body.scenario: Imagine it is some future year. India's current account deficit has widened to 3.2% of GDP after a sustained oil price spike. Import cover has slipped from 11 months to 7 months. Foreign investors have bought large amounts of Indian government bonds following index inclusion. Bank credit has grown at twice the pace of nominal GDP for three years, led by unsecured personal loans. Several mid-sized NBFCs rely heavily on commercial paper. Gross NPAs are still low.
body.prompt: Which warning lights are on, which stage of the crisis map does this most resemble, and what would you watch next?
body.modelAnswer: Lights on: external weakness, because a deficit of 3.2% of GDP is above the roughly 2.5% the RBI has described as sustainable, and import cover is falling, though 7 months is still well above the danger zone. Short-term funding, because large foreign holdings of Indian bonds can leave quickly, as in 2013, and NBFCs leaning on commercial paper echo 2018. Credit boom, because bank credit running at twice the pace of the economy, concentrated in unsecured loans, is a classic build-up signal. Hidden risk is possible, because low NPAs during rapid lending growth can be misleading, as the 2010s showed. Stage: this most resembles late build-up. There is no trigger or panic yet, and the external position is far stronger than 1991 or 2013, but several lights are turning on together. What to watch next: the next quarter's current account and import cover; weekly foreign portfolio flows in debt on the NSDL FPI Monitor; whether the RBI tightens rules on unsecured lending or considers activating the countercyclical capital buffer; spreads on NBFC commercial paper and bonds; rating outlooks on the fastest-growing lenders; and any sign of a trigger, such as a sudden US rate move or a large NBFC default. The point is not to predict a crash, but to notice when the conditions for one are building.

children.text: The dashboard tells you about the system. The lessons of this course also apply to your own money. This is general education, not a recommendation for your situation.

body.title: Lessons From a Century of Crises, Applied to Your Own Finances
steps: Know your deposit insurance: DICGC covers ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, so understand how much you hold above that in any one bank (1930s US, PMC Bank 2019)
Check whether anything you hold that looks like a deposit is actually not one, such as AT1 bonds or NBFC deposits (Yes Bank 2020, Credit Suisse 2023)
Avoid leverage you do not fully understand, including margin trading, and know your own wipeout point (LTCM 1998, Lehman 2008)
Look inside your debt funds: read the monthly portfolio and note credit risk and concentration (IL&FS 2018)
Be sceptical of unusually high yields, especially in another currency or from a single issuer (Russia 1998)
Keep enough cash or liquid assets that you are never forced to sell in a panic (every crisis in this course)
Avoid concentrating your wealth in one company, one sector or one product (PMC Bank 2019)

body.title: The Ideas That Explain Every Crisis

cards.definition: Build-up, trigger, panic and recognition, policy response, and repair and recovery.
Borrowing that magnifies losses. The wipeout point is capital divided by assets.
Owing in one currency while earning in another, as in 1982, 1997 and many other crises.
A central bank lending freely to sound institutions in a panic, from Bagehot to Draghi's whatever it takes.
Stress spreading through direct exposure, fire sales, funding freezes, wake-up calls and capital flight.
Forex reserves should at least cover external debt due within one year.

body.label: screener.in
body.description: Free financial data on NSE and BSE listed companies. Use it to check debt to equity, interest coverage and cash flows, the company-level version of the leverage and funding warning lights.

points: Across the 16 crises in this course, the most common main warning light was external weakness, followed by fragile short-term funding
The six warning lights to track are external weakness, short-term funding, credit booms, leverage, hidden or mispriced risk, and concentration

Useful rules of thumb include import cover above about 3 months, reserves at least covering short-term external debt, and a current account deficit the RBI has described as sustainable at about 2.5% of GDP
India's external position in 2026 is far stronger than in 1991, but domestic risks like the NBFC and PMC Bank crises can still occur when reserves are comfortable
The same lessons apply to personal finances: know your deposit insurance, avoid hidden leverage, read your debt fund portfolios and never concentrate everything in one place

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute investment advice or a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security or product. The rules of thumb are general guidelines, not predictions, and the recent readings will change. The hypothetical scenario does not describe any actual forecast. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser for advice specific to your situation.
